name: British Invasion
blurb: From Liverpool cellars to Ed Sullivan, the bands that conquered American radio.

questions.prompt: Which band drew an estimated 73 million Americans to The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964?
questions.fact: They opened with "All My Loving". Two months later, in April 1964, the Beatles held the top five spots on the Billboard Hot 100.

questions.prompt: Which Liverpool cellar club did the Beatles play almost 300 times between 1961 and 1963?
questions.fact: Brian Epstein first saw them at a lunchtime show there in November 1961 and soon became their manager.

questions.prompt: Which Beatles album cover shows the band crossing a London street on a zebra crossing?
questions.fact: Photographer Iain Macmillan took the picture on August 8, 1969, standing on a stepladder outside the EMI studios in St John's Wood.

questions.prompt: Which Beatle wrote "Something", a song Frank Sinatra praised as one of the great love songs?
questions.fact: It appeared on Abbey Road in 1969 and was the only Harrison song to become a Beatles A-side.

questions.prompt: Which 1967 Beatles album has a crowded cover collage designed by Peter Blake and Jann Haworth?
choices: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
questions.fact: The cover includes figures from Marlon Brando and Bob Dylan to Karl Marx and Oscar Wilde, along with waxwork Beatles.

questions.prompt: Which Beatle sings lead on "With a Little Help from My Friends" on Sgt. Pepper?
questions.fact: Lennon and McCartney wrote it for Ringo's limited vocal range, and the character he sings as is named Billy Shears.

questions.prompt: Where did the Beatles give their final public performance together, in January 1969?
choices: On top of the Apple building
In the middle of Hyde Park
questions.fact: Police shut down the lunchtime show on Savile Row after about 40 minutes, and the footage appears in the film Let It Be.

questions.prompt: Which band's shows ended with Pete Townshend smashing his guitar and Keith Moon wrecking his drums?
questions.fact: Townshend first broke a guitar by accident in 1964 when he hit a low ceiling at the Railway Hotel in Harrow, then made it part of the act.

questions.prompt: "Hey Jude" began as a song McCartney wrote to comfort which child?
questions.fact: McCartney wrote it while driving to visit Julian and his mother Cynthia after John left her. It was first called "Hey Jules".

questions.prompt: Which Newcastle band had a 1964 hit with a New Orleans folk song, "The House of the Rising Sun"?
questions.fact: Eric Burdon's raw vocal and Alan Price's organ drive the recording, which was cut in a single take.

questions.prompt: Keith Richards says the riff for which Stones hit came to him in his sleep in 1965?
questions.fact: Richards says he woke in a Florida motel, recorded the riff on a cassette, and went back to sleep. The tape holds the riff, followed by snoring.

questions.prompt: By his own account, how did Dave Davies of the Kinks get the raw guitar sound on "You Really Got Me"?
choices: He wired the amp to a car battery
He stuffed the amp with old towels
He turned the amp to face a wall
He cut the speaker with a razor
questions.fact: The damaged speaker produced the fuzzy snarl heard on the 1964 single, which is often cited as an early influence on heavy metal.

questions.prompt: The name "Beatles" was a play on the name of which band?
questions.fact: Lennon later said he wanted an insect name like the Crickets and added a "beat" pun. Earlier names included the Quarrymen and the Silver Beetles.

questions.prompt: Mick Jagger left which London school to pursue the Rolling Stones full time?
choices: The Slade School of Fine Art
questions.fact: Jagger studied there from 1961 and left in 1963. Keith Richards, for his part, had attended Sidcup Art College.

questions.prompt: Which Rolling Stone played the sitar on "Paint It Black"?
questions.fact: Jones was a multi-instrumentalist who also played marimba on "Under My Thumb" and dulcimer on "Lady Jane".

questions.prompt: Which producer oversaw almost every Beatles recording from 1962 to 1969?
questions.fact: Martin wrote the string arrangements for "Yesterday" and "Eleanor Rigby", and signed the band to EMI's Parlophone label after one audition.

questions.prompt: Most of the Beatles' debut album, Please Please Me, was recorded in how long?
choices: About ten hours in one day
questions.fact: The marathon session at Abbey Road took place on February 11, 1963, and ended with a raucous "Twist and Shout" with John Lennon's raw voice.

questions.prompt: A 15-year-old fan's letter to a Washington DJ in December 1963 pushed Capitol to rush which Beatles single into stores?
choices: I Want to Hold Your Hand
questions.fact: Marsha Albert wrote to DJ Carroll James, who played a British import on the air, and Capitol moved the release up from mid-January to December 26.

questions.prompt: Which guitarist joined the Yardbirds in 1966, following Eric Clapton and Jeff Beck?
questions.fact: Page later turned the band's last lineup into the New Yardbirds, which became Led Zeppelin in 1968.

questions.prompt: Which Hollies member left in 1968 to form Crosby, Stills & Nash?
questions.fact: Nash was frustrated that the Hollies refused to record his song "Marrakesh Express", which became a hit for his new group.

questions.prompt: Which British band's 1968 album Odessey and Oracle produced the 1969 US hit "Time of the Season" after they had split?
questions.fact: The album was recorded at Abbey Road, and the title was misspelled by the cover artist, who then left it as it was.

questions.prompt: Tom Jones's 1965 hit "It's Not Unusual" was reportedly written with which other singer in mind?
questions.fact: Songwriters Gordon Mills and Les Reed wrote it, and Jones's own demo of the song was strong enough that it became his signature.

questions.prompt: Which British band made 18 appearances on The Ed Sullivan Show, more than any other British act?
questions.fact: Leader Dave Clark kept ownership of the group's master recordings, and kept them off the market for decades.

questions.prompt: Which band recorded Bob Dylan's "The Mighty Quinn" in 1968, before Dylan himself released a version?
questions.fact: Dylan wrote it during the 1967 Basement Tapes sessions, and his own live version did not appear until the Isle of Wight recording on Self Portrait in 1970.

questions.prompt: The Troggs' 1966 hit "Wild Thing" features a solo on which unusual instrument?
questions.fact: Jimi Hendrix set his guitar on fire at the end of his version of the song at the 1967 Monterey Pop Festival.

questions.prompt: Ringo Starr wrote "Octopus's Garden" after a stay on whose yacht in Sardinia in 1968?
questions.fact: Ringo had left the band for a short time during the White Album sessions, and the yacht's captain told him about octopuses collecting shiny objects.

questions.prompt: What was the original title of the Kinks' "Waterloo Sunset", according to Ray Davies?
questions.fact: Davies has said the first idea was a nod to the Merseybeat scene, and the title changed when it became a London song.

questions.prompt: The Rolling Stones' "It's All Over Now", recorded at Chess Studios in 1964, was a cover of which group?
questions.fact: The Stones cut it at Chess Studios in Chicago in June 1964, and the song was written by Bobby Womack of the Valentinos.

questions.prompt: Which later 10cc member wrote "For Your Love", "Bus Stop" and "No Milk Today"?
questions.fact: The three songs were hits for the Yardbirds, the Hollies and Herman's Hermits respectively, and Gouldman later co-founded 10cc.

questions.prompt: At which Hamburg club did the Beatles open their first German residency, in August 1960?
questions.fact: Neighbors complained about the noise, and after a few weeks the band moved to the larger Kaiserkeller.

questions.prompt: The Beatles' first film took its title from a phrase Ringo Starr reportedly let slip. What was the film?
questions.fact: Ringo reportedly said the line after a long day of work, and Lennon and McCartney then wrote the title song within a day, with Richard Lester directing the 1964 film.

questions.prompt: In June 1967 the Beatles performed "All You Need Is Love" on a live TV broadcast carried by what technology?
questions.fact: The broadcast, called Our World, linked several countries and was reportedly watched by around 400 million people.

questions.prompt: Which Beatles song from Rubber Soul features a sitar played by George Harrison?
questions.fact: Harrison picked up the sitar on the film set of Help! and used it on the 1965 track, an early step in bringing Indian music into rock.

questions.prompt: Charlie Watts, the Rolling Stones' drummer, was a lifelong devoted fan of which kind of music?
questions.fact: Watts also led his own jazz groups on the side, and he kept a famously calm presence in the band.

questions.prompt: Which Beatles single was among the first releases on their own Apple label in 1968?
questions.fact: Apple was set up by the band to give artists freedom, and it also released music by Mary Hopkin and James Taylor.

questions.prompt: "Eleanor Rigby" features a string octet and no guitars. Which Beatles album is it on?
questions.fact: McCartney's story song from 1966 was recorded with studio string players while the other Beatles added vocal parts.

questions.prompt: George Harrison wrote "Here Comes the Sun" in the garden of which fellow guitarist?
questions.fact: Harrison has said he skipped a business meeting at Apple in spring 1969 and wrote the song at Clapton's house.

questions.prompt: Where did the Beatles play their final paid concert, in August 1966?
questions.fact: They had grown tired of touring in screaming crowds, and the rooftop show in 1969 was their last public appearance.

questions.prompt: At the Rolling Stones' July 1969 Hyde Park concert, Mick Jagger honored the late Brian Jones by releasing what?
questions.fact: Jones died two days before the show, and Jagger first read aloud from a poem by Shelley.

questions.prompt: Tony Hatch reportedly found the idea for Petula Clark's "Downtown" on his first visit to which city?
questions.fact: Hatch has said the sound of the busy streets sparked the song, and Clark's 1964 recording became a signature hit.

questions.prompt: Paul McCartney's working title for "Yesterday" was what?
questions.fact: The melody came to him in a dream, and he used silly placeholder words until the real lyric arrived.

questions.prompt: Which Small Faces singer went on to co-found Humble Pie?
questions.fact: Marriott left in 1968 and teamed up with Peter Frampton, while the rest of the Small Faces later became the Faces with Rod Stewart.

questions.prompt: The organ line of "A Whiter Shade of Pale" is often said to echo a piece by which composer?
questions.fact: Procol Harum's Gary Brooker has acknowledged a Bach influence, and Matthew Fisher's organ work gave the 1967 song its hymn-like feel.

questions.prompt: The Rolling Stones' tongue-and-lips logo was designed in 1970 by a student at which London school?
choices: The Slade School of Fine Art
questions.fact: John Pasche was reportedly paid a small fee at first, and the design appeared on Sticky Fingers in 1971.

questions.prompt: Which American producer in London worked on early records by both the Kinks and the Who?
questions.fact: Talmy produced "You Really Got Me" and the Who's early singles, and the hard sound he helped capture shaped British rock.

questions.prompt: John Lennon reportedly wrote "I Am the Walrus" with deliberately nonsensical lyrics after hearing that a school was doing what with Beatles songs?

stories.title: Four Lads on Ed Sullivan
stories.dek: The night America met the Beatles
stories.body:
On a Friday in February 1964, a plane carrying four young men from Liverpool landed at New York's recently renamed John F. Kennedy Airport. About three thousand screaming teenagers were waiting for them. The Beatles had arrived in America, and the country had been waiting for something to cheer about since the assassination of President Kennedy less than three months before.

Until the end of 1963, American record labels had treated the band as a minor curiosity. Capitol, the American arm of EMI, had refused several of their records. Then something changed. A teenage fan in Washington, D.C. wrote to a local DJ, who got hold of a copy of "I Want to Hold Your Hand" and played it on the air. The phones lit up. Capitol rushed the release forward to late December, and by the time the band flew to New York, the record was the No. 1 single in America.

Ed Sullivan, the stiff but influential host of a Sunday variety show on CBS, had seen the Beatles' reception at Heathrow Airport a few months before and booked them for three appearances. The first was on February 9, 1964, from his theater on Broadway. The show opened with the band's set at about eight in the evening, and about 73 million people watched, a record for American television at the time.

The Beatles played "All My Loving", "Till There Was You" and "She Loves You" before the break, and then "I Saw Her Standing There" and "I Want to Hold Your Hand" afterward. The studio audience, mostly teenage girls, screamed so loudly that the music was barely audible. Paul McCartney sang "Till There Was You", a show tune from The Music Man. The cameras flashed names beneath each face, and under John Lennon's was a note that he was already married.

What happened next was a flood. Within weeks, the Beatles held the top five positions on the Billboard Hot 100, a first for any act. American teenagers formed their own bands, and hundreds of British groups, including the Rolling Stones, the Animals, the Kinks and the Who, followed them across the Atlantic. Critics called it the British Invasion, and it reshaped American pop music for the rest of the decade.

Years later, many musicians, Tom Petty and Billy Joel among them, would say the same thing: they watched that night and decided what to do with their lives. A half hour of television had set off a generation of guitar players.

stories.title: Satisfaction
stories.dek: A riff from a dream, a fuzz box and a first US No. 1
stories.body:
In May 1965 the Rolling Stones were on tour in the United States and doing well, but they had not yet scored an American No. 1 single. Keith Richards has told the story many times of what happened next, at a motel in Clearwater, Florida. He says he woke in the middle of the night, picked up an acoustic guitar, and played a riff into a cassette recorder he kept beside his bed. Then he went back to sleep. In the morning he found the tape. It held about two minutes of that riff, followed by forty minutes of snoring.

Richards thought of it as a rough sketch, perhaps a part for a horn section. Mick Jagger wrote the lyrics by the motel pool. They were a blunt, funny complaint about advertising, sexual frustration and a world that seemed to promise everything. Nothing in pop at the time had sounded quite so sour.

The band tried it first at Chess Studios in Chicago, the home of their heroes Muddy Waters and Chuck Berry, with an acoustic arrangement. Nobody liked the result. A couple of days later they tried again at RCA Studios in Hollywood. This time Richards used a new piece of equipment, a Gibson Maestro Fuzz-Tone, which turned his guitar into a buzzing, snarling machine. The effect had been on the market since 1962 and sold poorly. Within months of the Stones' single, the store shelves were bare.

The band thumped through the song. Their manager Andrew Loog Oldham liked it at once, but Richards was not sure and wanted a different version. Jagger and Oldham pushed ahead. The single came out in June 1965, and by July it reached the top of the Billboard chart, the band's first American No. 1.

It also made the Stones into something different from the Beatles. If the Fab Four were charming, the Stones were dangerous, and their record sounded like a complaint from someone who did not expect to be answered. The riff became one of the best-known figures in rock, copied by garage bands for decades, and the song became the Stones' signature number on tour.

Richards, for his part, has often said he credits the song to a dream, a gift that arrived in his sleep, and that he does not know where it came from.

stories.title: The Zombies' Lost Masterpiece
stories.dek: A band that broke up before its biggest hit
stories.body:
The Zombies were from St Albans, north of London, and had a hit in 1964 with "She's Not There". By 1967 they were struggling. Their later singles had not sold, the schedule of touring was heavy, and money was tight. Even so, keyboardist Rod Argent, bassist Chris White and singer Colin Blunstone decided to make an album the way they wanted.

They signed a small contract with CBS and booked time at Abbey Road, the same studio the Beatles had made their records in. The budget was tiny, so they had to be quick and careful. They used the studio's Mellotron, which let them play tape-based string and flute sounds from a keyboard, and the engineers who had worked with the Beatles, including Geoff Emerick, helped them with the sound. White and Argent wrote nearly all the songs, and the band layered their harmonies on top of baroque keyboard parts.

The finished album, Odessey and Oracle, was rich and strange. It had songs about war, death and loneliness, and it also had warm pop melodies. The cover was painted by a friend, Terry Quirk, who misspelled the word Odyssey, and the band decided to keep it.

By the time the sessions finished, the group had already come to the end of the road. The band decided it could not go on, and the Zombies broke up in December 1967, months before their album came out. CBS released it in Britain in April 1968, and it vanished almost at once.

The story would have ended there, but in the United States Al Kooper, then working as a producer and musician for CBS, heard a copy and loved it. He insisted the label release it. A single, "Time of the Season", with Blunstone's breathy vocal and Argent's organ, was issued in the United States, and in early 1969 it began to climb the charts. It reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100. The band had split more than a year earlier.

Odessey and Oracle slowly found its audience, and critics now place it among the finest albums of the era. Argent and Blunstone later reunited and played the album in full on stage, four decades after it was recorded.

stories.title: Hey Jules, Hey Jude
stories.dek: A song for a five-year-old, and a seven-minute single.
stories.body:
In the summer of 1968 John Lennon's marriage to Cynthia was ending, and Paul McCartney worried about their five-year-old son, Julian. McCartney has said he started working out a song in the car as he drove out to Weybridge to visit them. The first version was addressed to Jules, and he later changed the name to Jude because it sounded better. He has also said that the name Jude may have been inspired by a character in the musical Oklahoma!

The words were meant as comfort for a child going through a hard time, but the song works for anyone. When McCartney played it for Lennon, Lennon reportedly took one of the lines as a message to himself, a nudge to move forward with his new life.

The Beatles recorded the song on July 31, 1968, at Trident Studios in London, which had a modern eight-track machine. The arrangement starts with McCartney alone at the piano and builds slowly as the rest of the band joins in. After the second half the song turns into a long, repeating chant, and McCartney brought in a 36-piece orchestra and asked the players to sing and clap along during the finale.

The record ran more than seven minutes, which was far longer than most singles of the time, and people at the label reportedly wondered whether radio would play it. The Beatles were confident that it would, and they were right. Apple Records released it on August 30, 1968, as one of the label's first four singles, alongside Mary Hopkin's Those Were the Days.

The band also filmed a promotional clip at Twickenham Film Studios in September, with a studio audience of fans who were invited to join in on the chorus. It was shown on David Frost's television program, and its warm, informal feel helped establish the song as a sing-along.

Julian Lennon has talked about the song over the years, and he has said that he learned only years later that it was written for him. That changed how he heard it.

stories.title: My Generation
stories.dek: A young band, a stuttering singer and a two-minute declaration.
stories.body:
In 1965 the Who were a loud young band from London with a loyal following among the mods, the sharp-dressed teenagers who rode scooters and went out dancing every night. Guitarist Pete Townshend wanted a song that spoke for them, and he wrote My Generation as a short statement of impatience with the adult world.

The song was recorded in October 1965 at IBC Studios in London, with American producer Shel Talmy in the control room. It is built on a hard, simple riff and a call and response between the singer and the band. Roger Daltrey delivers the lines with a stutter that gives the vocal a nervous, impatient edge, and the band answers with sharp, shouted syllables. The stutter suggests a young man so frustrated that he can barely get the words out. The BBC reportedly had concerns about it, because it might offend people who stammer in real life.

In the middle of the song there is a bass solo from John Entwistle, which was unusual for a pop single of the era. It shows how a bassist could step out as a lead player. Keith Moon's drumming is wild and busy, and Townshend's guitar chords are slashing and loud.

The line about hoping to die before getting old became a motto for the young listeners of the time. Townshend has said that he was only writing from the viewpoint of a young man, and as the years passed he and his bandmates had to live with the line while growing older themselves. The song stayed in the Who's live set for decades, and the extended versions often ended with the band smashing their instruments.

My Generation was released in late 1965, and it helped establish the Who as the loudest and most restless act of the British Invasion. A short song, a hard riff and a stuttering voice were enough to make a statement that has not worn out.

stories.title: A Whiter Shade of Pale
stories.dek: An organ that sounds like church and a lawsuit that took decades.
stories.body:
In the spring of 1967 a new British band called Procol Harum released a single that sounded like nothing else on the radio. Lyricist Keith Reid had written a set of strange, dreamlike words, and pianist and singer Gary Brooker set them to music. Reid has said the title came from a phrase he overheard at a party. The band's name, according to the usual story, came from the name of a friend's cat.

The music rests on a slow, stately chord pattern that many listeners hear as an echo of Bach. Brooker has acknowledged a Bach influence. Over that pattern, organist Matthew Fisher plays a long, singing line on a Hammond organ that makes the whole record feel like a hymn. Producer Denny Cordell recorded the song at Olympic Studios in London in the spring of 1967, and the single came out in May.

The reaction was strong. The song arrived in the summer that rock music was growing more ambitious, and it helped show that a pop single could be moody and mysterious. The lyrics are full of images that listeners have argued over for decades, and the band has never offered one clear explanation. Its popularity spread through Europe and North America, and it became a favorite of slow dances and late-night radio.

The story did not end there. Decades later Fisher claimed that he had helped write the music, especially the organ melody that opens the song. In 2006 a British court agreed that he was a co-author of the music, and the ruling gave him a share of the future royalties. The decision was upheld on appeal. The case drew new attention to the contribution of players who shape a song in the studio.

Whatever the outcome, the record remains one of the most recognizable sounds of 1967. The organ line, the stately pace and the cryptic words have given it a long life, from jukeboxes to movie soundtracks and wedding receptions.

stories.title: Washington Coliseum, February 11, 1964
stories.dek: The Beatles' first American concert, in the round and in the snow.
stories.body:
Two days after the Ed Sullivan Show, the Beatles gave their first concert in the United States. The date was February 11, 1964, and the place was the Washington Coliseum, a big sports arena in the capital. A snowstorm had made flying difficult, so the band took a train from New York to Washington.

The arena was not built for music. The stage was set up like a boxing ring in the middle of the floor, and the audience sat on all four sides, with thousands of fans screaming loudly enough that the band could barely hear itself. The crew reportedly had to turn Ringo Starr's drum platform by hand during the set so that every part of the crowd had a view of the group.

The concert lasted about half an hour. The Beatles played songs they knew well from their British shows, including She Loves You, and the crowd of some eight thousand people shouted along. Fans also threw jelly beans at the stage, because George Harrison had mentioned in an interview that he liked jelly babies, a British candy, and American fans reportedly looked for the nearest equivalent. The band is said to have found that the candy hurt when it landed.

The show was filmed, and a version was reportedly shown in movie theaters in the United States, which gave many fans a chance to see the group who could not get tickets. The next night the Beatles played two shows at Carnegie Hall in New York, a more formal setting that was a sharp contrast to the Coliseum.

Looking back, the evening looks modest compared with the stadium tours that came later. But it shows how fast things were moving in 1964. A band that had arrived in America only four days earlier was already playing to a full arena, in a snowstorm, with sweets bouncing off the stage.

stories.title: Monterey Pop, June 1967
stories.dek: A weekend of Hendrix, the Who and a flaming guitar.
stories.body:
In June 1967 a three-day festival was held at the fairgrounds in Monterey, California. It was organized by a group of musicians and music figures including John Phillips of the Mamas and the Papas and producer Lou Adler, and it became a model for later festivals. The Monterey International Pop Festival gave audiences an early taste of what the Summer of Love would sound like, and it was filmed by documentary maker D. A. Pennebaker.

Two British acts made a strong impression. The Who were not yet stars in the United States, and the festival gave them a major stage. They played a short, loud set and closed with My Generation, and at the end Pete Townshend smashed his guitar while Keith Moon kicked over his drum kit, with smoke bombs reportedly going off around the stage. For many in the audience, it was the first time they had seen anything like it.

Jimi Hendrix was an American guitarist who had made his name in London, and Monterey was his first major appearance back home. Rolling Stones guitarist Brian Jones came on stage to introduce him, calling him one of the most exciting performers he had heard. Hendrix played a set of blues-based songs and finished with a wild version of Wild Thing, a song that had been a hit for the Troggs. At the end he knelt in front of his guitar, poured lighter fluid on it and set it on fire.

Backstage stories grew up around the show. One is that the Who and Hendrix argued over who should go on first, since neither wanted to follow the other, and that a coin toss reportedly decided it. It is a good story, and it fits the competitive atmosphere of the weekend.

The festival also featured Otis Redding, Janis Joplin with Big Brother and the Holding Company, Ravi Shankar and many others. Hendrix's performance gave him a reputation in his own country, and the Who made a strong impression with American fans. The weekend showed that British and American rock were now moving together.

covers.title: Twist and Shout
covers.note: Phil Spector produced the Top Notes' 1961 version, and the Isley Brothers had the 1962 hit. The Beatles reportedly recorded theirs in one take at the end of the Please Please Me session.

covers.title: You Really Got a Hold on Me
covers.note: Smokey Robinson wrote it and the Miracles had the 1962 hit. The Beatles put it on With the Beatles, with John Lennon and George Harrison sharing the vocal.

covers.title: Needles and Pins
covers.note: Jackie DeShannon recorded the Sonny Bono and Jack Nitzsche song in 1963. The Searchers' jangling version, released in 1964, reached number one in the UK.

covers.title: Not Fade Away
covers.note: Buddy Holly's group the Crickets released it in 1957. The Stones leaned on a Bo Diddley style beat and took it into the UK top three in early 1964.

covers.title: It's All Over Now
covers.note: The Valentinos were a family group led by Bobby Womack, who wrote it. The Stones' cover gave them their first UK number one that summer.

covers.title: Shout
covers.note: The Isley Brothers released it in 1959, and it reportedly grew out of an ad lib on stage. Lulu was about fifteen when she and her band recorded it, and it became her first hit.

covers.title: Baby, Please Don't Go
covers.note: Big Joe Williams recorded it in 1935, and it became a blues standard. Them's 1964 version, sung by a young Van Morrison, turned it into a garage rock staple.

covers.title: Do Wah Diddy Diddy
covers.note: Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich wrote it, and the Exciters recorded it in 1963. Manfred Mann's 1964 version reached number one in both the UK and the US.

covers.title: Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood
covers.note: Simone introduced the song on Broadway-Blues-Ballads. The Animals followed with a faster rock arrangement.

covers.title: Bring It On Home to Me
covers.note: Cooke's original has Lou Rawls answering his vocal. The Animals recorded their version with Mickie Most.

covers.title: Boys
covers.note: The Shirelles released it on the reverse of 'Will You Love Me Tomorrow'. Ringo takes the lead on the Beatles' version.

covers.title: He Ain't Heavy, He's My Brother
covers.album: He Ain't Heavy, He's My Brother
covers.note: Gordon released the song before the Hollies. Elton John plays piano on their recording.

covers.title: Sweets for My Sweet
covers.note: Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman wrote it. Tony Hatch produced the Searchers' version.

covers.title: I'm into Something Good
covers.note: The Cookies singer released the Goffin-King song before the Manchester band recorded it with Mickie Most.

covers.title: Hippy Hippy Shake
covers.note: Romero wrote and recorded the song for Del-Fi. The Liverpool band's version followed four years later.

covers.title: It's All Over Now, Baby Blue
covers.note: Dylan closed Bringing It All Back Home with the song. Van Morrison sings Them's version.
